FROM MY DESK   This morning, we’re taking you inside a late-night party central to the saga: At a Taipei bar in 2024 , Alice Huang told fellow executives, “Jensen’s a great friend of mine.” She sent a text, and minutes later the Nvidia CEO arrived for a whiskey.

   Before long, U.S. and Asian authorities were investigating whether her firm, Megaspeed, was illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China, and probing her suspected intelligence ties.

   The chip giant lost roughly $200 billion in market value yesterday after launching an inquiry into their affair, and the reckoning now imperils Jensen Huang’s leadership of Nvidia and the AI industry that depends on its technology and financial help.

   The scandal also lays bare an extraordinary governance vacuum : Nvidia lacks a chairman or succession plan, and it denied Huang’s relationship only for him to later acknowledge it.

   • California voters rejected a proposed billionaire tax , ending a heated fight over what could have been the nation’s first modern wealth tax.

   • Democrats are wasting no time investigating corporate America’s biggest names.

   • Trump’s plan to lower drug prices in the U.S. is leading to fewer new drugs in Europe.

Here’s why.   America’s $100 billion beef industry is undergoing a painful downsizing, and it’s poised to make high meat prices a long-term reality . After years of economic turmoil and droughts, the U.S. cattle herd has shrunk to its smallest level in 75 years. The supply shock is driving up steak and hamburger prices at grocery stores and restaurants to record highs—conditions that could last well into the next decade, given how long it takes to replenish a herd. Beef prices have become the poster child for food inflation and a Trump administration obsession. Everyone is divided on how to fix it. Interviews with ranchers, meatpackers and policymakers reveal a fractured supply chain with few good answers, reports Patrick Thomas.

       5. REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK   James Marson: I first learned who Pvt. Kostyantyn Vlasenko was while scrolling through social media one morning a few weeks ago. The unit that saved him had published footage of him being evacuated by a drone, describing it as a first in the history of warfare.

   This was a rescue story, but also one of a drone nearly killing a man and another drone saving him.

   On Oct. 30, I met up with my colleague Nikita Nikolaienko and photographer Emanuele Satolli in Lviv, where we sat down with Vlasenko over two days.

   I interviewed him in Ukrainian, which helped establish a quick rapport. Vlasenko was remarkably open, and I was struck by his humor a s he recounted how he survived holed up alone in a school boiler room on the front line of the war with Russia.

   While there’s been a lot of focus on him cutting his foot off to survive, what fascinated me was how he coped mentally as well as physically: He befriended animals that wandered through and gave them names, and cracked jokes with his unit on the radio. The animals were part of a space he created for himself that at one point he described as “comfortable.”

   Vlasenko kept a photo of his cats and a key ring with an image of his wife’s eyes with him on the front lines. And he told us that’s one thing that kept him going—a connection to his everyday life.

   With all the advances in drone tech, what does it actually mean to be a soldier on the front lines? Through his story, I hope we’ve shown what it is really like to be a human in a robot war.

The Affair That Turned Into a National Security Nightmare
 
Plus, California voters reject an unprecedented tax on billionaires, and parents are suing schools because their kids got bad grades
 
 
ANTHONY WALLACE/AFP/GETTY IMAGES
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

This morning, we’re taking you inside a late-night party central to the saga: At a Taipei bar in 2024, Alice Huang told fellow executives, “Jensen’s a great friend of mine.” She sent a text, and minutes later the Nvidia CEO arrived for a whiskey.

 

Before long, U.S. and Asian authorities were investigating whether her firm, Megaspeed, was illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China, and probing her suspected intelligence ties.

 

The chip giant lost roughly $200 billion in market value yesterday after launching an inquiry into their affair, and the reckoning now imperils Jensen Huang’s leadership of Nvidia and the AI industry that depends on its technology and financial help.

 

The scandal also lays bare an extraordinary governance vacuum: Nvidia lacks a chairman or succession plan, and it denied Huang’s relationship only for him to later acknowledge it.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• President Trump said Huang told him he didn’t know that the industry executive he had an intimate relationship with was a suspected spy.

 

• California voters rejected a proposed billionaire tax, ending a heated fight over what could have been the nation’s first modern wealth tax.

 

• Democrats are wasting no time investigating corporate America’s biggest names.

 

• Trump’s plan to lower drug prices in the U.S. is leading to fewer new drugs in Europe.

 

• ExxonMobil signed a preliminary deal to explore investments in Venezuela’s oil patch, negotiating a potential return to the country nearly two decades after its exit.

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

High beef prices are here to stay. Here’s why.

 

America’s $100 billion beef industry is undergoing a painful downsizing, and it’s poised to make high meat prices a long-term reality. After years of economic turmoil and droughts, the U.S. cattle herd has shrunk to its smallest level in 75 years. The supply shock is driving up steak and hamburger prices at grocery stores and restaurants to record highs—conditions that could last well into the next decade, given how long it takes to replenish a herd. Beef prices have become the poster child for food inflation and a Trump administration obsession. Everyone is divided on how to fix it. Interviews with ranchers, meatpackers and policymakers reveal a fractured supply chain with few good answers, reports Patrick Thomas.

 
 
 

5. REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK

 

James Marson: I first learned who Pvt. Kostyantyn Vlasenko was while scrolling through social media one morning a few weeks ago. The unit that saved him had published footage of him being evacuated by a drone, describing it as a first in the history of warfare.

 

This was a rescue story, but also one of a drone nearly killing a man and another drone saving him.

 

On Oct. 30, I met up with my colleague Nikita Nikolaienko and photographer Emanuele Satolli in Lviv, where we sat down with Vlasenko over two days.

 

I interviewed him in Ukrainian, which helped establish a quick rapport. Vlasenko was remarkably open, and I was struck by his humor as he recounted how he survived holed up alone in a school boiler room on the front line of the war with Russia.

 

While there’s been a lot of focus on him cutting his foot off to survive, what fascinated me was how he coped mentally as well as physically: He befriended animals that wandered through and gave them names, and cracked jokes with his unit on the radio. The animals were part of a space he created for himself that at one point he described as “comfortable.”

 

Vlasenko kept a photo of his cats and a key ring with an image of his wife’s eyes with him on the front lines. And he told us that’s one thing that kept him going—a connection to his everyday life.

 

With all the advances in drone tech, what does it actually mean to be a soldier on the front lines? Through his story, I hope we’ve shown what it is really like to be a human in a robot war.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

Watch how a 15-year-old football star and his parents navigate the business of NIL deals.

 
 
Photo Illustration: Ryan Trefes/WSJ, Madeleine Peters/WSJ, Robson Lopes
 

Amateur athletes’ ability to sign endorsement deals that monetize their name, image and likeness has pumped billions of dollars into college sports. Now it is coming for high-school athletes. For some parents and coaches, NIL deals create welcome opportunities for students to offset the growing costs of elite youth sports. Others, especially in the six states that still restrict NIL activity before college, think allowing teenage athletes to cash in on their personal brands takes the increasing professionalization of amateur sports too far.

8. THE NUMBER

The expected rise in Wall Street compensation this year, according to a report from Options Group, as firms cash in on market volatility and flashy stock-market debuts. Last year, the average Wall Street bonus rose 6% to a record $246,900, while average total compensation exceeded $561,770, according to New York state Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Parents are suing schools because their kids got bad grades.

 

In Silicon Valley and beyond, families are pressuring teachers or calling lawyers over classroom clashes, from a recess squabble to an essay flagged as “76% AI.” Esther Wojcicki, a retired Palo Alto teacher and author of “How to Raise Successful People,” said parents have a newfound sense of self-righteousness in protecting their children—and the friction is pushing some teachers over the edge.
